title: Who Should Make the First Offer?
text:
Negotiation folklore often advises letting the other side name a number first. In 2001 Adam Galinsky and Thomas Mussweiler put that advice to the test with MBA students at Northwestern University's Kellogg School of Management.

Students were paired as buyer and seller in a simulated negotiation over the sale of a pharmaceutical plant. Whoever made the first offer, buyer or seller, tended to end up with the better deal. The first offer worked as an anchor: the final agreed price was closely correlated with it. An ambitious opening number pulled the whole negotiation toward the side that made it.

The researchers then looked for ways to resist the anchor. In further studies, they asked the side receiving the first offer to focus on particular information before responding. Some were asked to think about the other side's alternatives to the deal and the lowest price the other side might accept. Others were asked to focus on their own target price, their ideal outcome. Either kind of focus, pointing attention to information inconsistent with the opponent's anchor, wiped out the advantage of the first mover. The final prices no longer tracked the first offer.

The authors concluded that making the first offer is often an advantage, especially when you are well prepared and the other side is not. But a negotiator who receives an extreme first offer can neutralize it by deliberately thinking about the facts that contradict it.
lesson: If you know the value of what is being negotiated, consider making the first, ambitious but defensible offer. If the other side opens first, refocus at once on your own target and their alternatives.
source: Galinsky, A. D., and Mussweiler, T. (2001). First offers as anchors: The role of perspective-taking and negotiator focus. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 81(4), 657-669.
